item.description:
作者：Dan Shipper 账号：@danshipper 简介：ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI
Everybody is talking about honeypot! Was it a honeypot always or merely at the end, as a form of circumstance? But this is precisely the trap. *sniffs* These are merely the *surface* of the situation.
What is the real infidelity? America tells Nvidia: you are married to national security, you must not sell your most powerful chips to China. But in the same breath it says: you are the great hero of American capitalism! Sell as many chips as possible! And Jensen says: of course, darling, I will be faithful. Then, late at night, *sniffs* he finds a way to remain faithful.
So you see, Jensen is not cheating on the system. Cheating on his wife? Yes. The system? No. He is the only one who has been faithful to it!
The system itself wants two incompatible things: to contain China and to dominate the Chinese market. And now we are shocked, shocked, that somebody got caught in a compromising position. *sniffs* And so on.
This is the true infidelity. This is the real honeypot.

item.title: What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate. UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. Agents are the new design engine...
item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn?
The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate.
UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously.
Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine.
I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate.
Enjoy!

item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Ok this is a big deal. We’ve been testing Gemini 4 Hydrogen in early access with the Box AI Complex Work Eval, and it’s a serious jump for fast models.
Hydrogen is 5 percentage points better in accuracy than Gemini 3.8 Flash. That alone would be a great boost in capability, but possibly more importantly it did the tasks in less than half the time with about 12% fewer tokens on a typical task.
For this eval, we give the Box Agent Hydrogen as a model for a series of complex tasks that represent real world work with enterprise documents across finance, consulting, life sciences, and other industries. Hydrogen will be a great model for a lot of efficient but complex tasks across these fields.
Gemini team is definitely cooking. Hydrogen will be rolling out in the Box AI Studio shortly so any customer can build a custom agent with it.

item.title: Powering AI-Driven Drug Discovery with President of Isomorphic Labs Max Jaderberg
item.description:
播客：No Priors
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:24 The large part of the industry makes medicines is this very empirically driven process. Where things really fail is in the clinic because we never could see the problems until we get to the point where we put these drugs in patients and we say, Oh no, like, there's toxicity that we didn't account for. And so the really big opportunity is to have much more of that understanding before you go into patients. How can we bring all of that drug discovery work onto a computer? So how can we get out of the real world?
Speaker 1 | 00:24 - 00:33 I'd be really disappointed if we fast forward even five years' time. Like, the predictive understanding of disease biology has not step changed in, like, a massive way.
Speaker 2 | 00:33 - 01:07 Do you have a prediction on when you think, for example, eighty percent of human cancers will be treatable? Today, know priors were joined by Max Jadberg. Max is the president and part of the founding team of Isomorphic Labs. Isomorphic is backed by Alphabet and a variety of other investors, and its goal is to solve all disease, which is very exciting as a topic. We're going to talk a little bit about the role of AI in the future of biopharma, human health, longevity.
Speaker 2 | 01:07 - 01:22 And Max, of course, has a background in machine learning. He has a PhD in the topic working on machine vision. Eventually sold a company to Google DeepMind, rose up the ranks there, and now is president of isomorphic. So very excited to have this conversation. Max, thank you so much for joining us today on Priors.
Speaker 1 | 01:22 - 01:23 No. It's such a pleasure to be here.
Speaker 2 | 01:23 - 01:50 Thank you. Isomorphic, I think, is is one of the more fascinating companies right now that's happening in technology in general. Alphabet is a major shareholder and sort of sponsor. Demis, who pioneered a lot of models at DeepMind and other places, which I believe you sold the company to before, you know, really helped with the inception and setup and now running of the company. And you folks are tackling one of the biggest problems that's left for humanity to tackle, which is human health.
Speaker 2 | 01:50 - 01:55 Could you tell me a bit about how you came to work on this company, and what was the motive force to starting it?
Speaker 1 | 01:55 - 02:13 I was part of the founding team of Isomorphic Labs. I was at DeepMind for a long time beforehand. You know, personally, I was working on early days of generative models, language models, deep reinforcement learning, all of the big, you know, game playing challenge problems. Those were my jam. My AlphaGo, AlphaStar.
Speaker 1 | 02:13 - 02:25 And it got to the point where, you know, we were we were going after these, like, know, quote unquote impossible problems at that point in time. You know, this is probably twenty eighteen, nineteen, that's
Speaker 2 | 02:25 - 02:27 sort It's like gameplay and can AI beat video games? Exactly.
Speaker 1 | 02:27 - 02:40 You know, at that point in time, you know, we were still trying to prove to the world that AI was even a thing. Right? Mhmm. And so we were going after these impossible problems, and I could see, you know, firsthand, like, how to... Like, just systematically how to solve these.
Speaker 1 | 02:40 - 02:58 Mhmm. And it got to the point for me personally where it's like, okay. Sure. We're not at AGI yet, but we clearly have this amazing, you know, set of technologies, you know, in deep learning and reinforcement learning. And, you know, what are the problems we really need to be focusing this stuff on?
Speaker 1 | 02:58 - 03:44 And I was, you know, I was thinking all of this. Of course, Demis was thinking all of this. At the same time, we're seeing the AlphaFold results, you know, the first embers of that starting to emerge and really starting to see, for us, this was like the first proof of concept that you could get a deep learning model that generalizes in, you know, a meaningful space in biology. And so that was really the proof of concepts that gave us conviction that actually, you know, now is the right time to go after this, you know, the big mission of, you know, changing the way that we think about human health, you know, going after solving all disease, and that's gonna take, like, a really substantial effort. And that warrants its own company, its own culture, you know, specific people of different disciplines coming together for this and and the ability to run really fast on that.
Speaker 1 | 03:44 - 03:48 So that was the genesis of isomorphic labs in in about 2021.
Speaker 2 | 03:48 - 03:56 Oh, amazing. Yeah. Your background really started off more on the deep learning side and AI modeling side, and I believe you sold the company to DeepMind in... Was it 2014?
Speaker 1 | 03:56 - 03:57 Yeah. That's right.
Speaker 2 | 03:57 - 04:07 So quite early. I mean, you were at this stuff before people realized how important it was, or many people realized how important it was. Tell... Could you tell me a little bit more about sort of the journey you took, how you got there? What was interested in it to begin with?
Speaker 1 | 04:07 - 04:23 Yeah. I mean, I I I come from an engineering background, ended up almost by accident doing a PhD, in computer vision, and this was actually just at the turning point. I think I started my PhD pre AlexNet.
Speaker 2 | 04:23 - 04:25 Oh, because AlexNet was 2012? Yeah.
Speaker 1 | 04:25 - 04:30 Is it? Yeah. Exactly. And then I saw that emerge. I was like, wow, this is awesome.
Speaker 1 | 04:30 - 05:02 I remember speaking to Jan Lakun about convolution neural neural convnets, and I was like, we need to translate this into the core computer vision space that we're we're working on in Oxford. And, yes, ended up developing all of these methods. We ended up having the ImageNet winning network of of twenty fourteen, best object recognition, text detection, all of this sort of stuff. And I had a company... Like, built a company in this space, computer vision as a service, and trying to raise money.
Speaker 1 | 05:02 - 05:22 And at that point in time, you know, Demis and DeepMind had just sold to Google. So trying to raise money very and very quickly ended up just speaking to Demis Asabis asking for angel investment and he was like, well, why don't you just come to DeepMind to solve AGI? I was like, what's AGI? Uh-huh. But Sovic and the journey into DeepMind and and everything there.
Speaker 2 | 05:22 - 05:44 Yeah. Amazing. And your focus now is basically a vertically integrated company that's doing everything from models to the biology, and the idea is to find drugs that can help people with different aspects of human health. And so if you look at the pharma industry, one of the things that I think is really striking... I've graphed this out in the past, where if you look at the number of new drug approvals per year, it's roughly flat.
Speaker 2 | 05:45 - 06:04 But that's despite an explosion in knowledge. So all these scientific papers have sort of expedited in terms of the number of papers. The number papers have gone up 10, 20x during that period. The number of new modalities, the type of new drugs that you can do has gone So there's antibody based drugs, there's small molecules, there's proteins, there's peptides, there's all these new ways you can treat drugs. The price has gone way up.
Speaker 2 | 06:04 - 06:23 It went from $100 a few $100,000,000 per drug to $1,500,000,000 It went from eight or nine years to fifteen years. So every metric has gotten worse. While the number of things have gotten flat, the knowledge base has exploded, the number of types of molecules that you can do has gone up. Why is that? Why has it been so static despite all that progress in other ways?
Speaker 1 | 06:24 - 06:53 Yeah. It's crazy to see just how it keeps getting harder and harder to make new medicines more and more expensive longer and longer. And, you know, I I I think ther...
